docs.title: streamlit-recommenders
docs.text:
Turn a recommender into an interactive web demo that others can inspect: pick a user, see their history and the model's recommendations, give feedback, compare models side by side.

You supply pandas tables and a function (or object) that returns ranked item ids. The library provides the Streamlit app around it: session profile, caching, layouts, model comparison, and helpers for metrics and plots. It contains no models of its own.

Offline metrics say how a model scores on average; they do not show what it recommends to a given user or how it reacts to new feedback. A demo shows that, but building one is frontend work. This library makes it a few lines of Python, so a demo can be published with a paper.

docs.text: Page Read it when Getting started you want a running demo Recommender contract you connect your own model Data contract you prepare your own tables Feedback & session you need to know what Like, Dislike, Skip and seen-filtering do Inspection views you add metrics or plots below the demo Architecture you want the internals Examples you want runnable code for each plug-in form Datasets you need MovieLens, goodbooks or TMDB posters Training & artifacts you train elsewhere and load weights API reference you look up a function

docs.title: scores(user_id, session_items=None, history_window=None, disliked_items=None, dislike_weight=1.0, **params)
docs.text:
Score every item for user_id using the loaded artifact.

For sequential models, scores come from the weight row of the most recent (anchor) item; otherwise from a user profile vector multiplied by the weight matrix. Falls back to popularity when no signal exists. Dislikes only adjust a score the model produced: on their own they are no profile, so the popularity fallback stays untouched.

Parameters:

Name Type Description Default user_id str | int

Id of the user to score items for.

required session_items list | None

Items selected during the current session.

None history_window int | str | None

Number of most recent history items to keep, or "All"/None to use the full history.

None disliked_items list | None

Items disliked during the current session; each subtracts dislike_weight times its weight row.

None dislike_weight float

Strength of one dislike relative to one positive item (0 ignores dislikes).

1.0 **params

Additional parameters (ignored).

{}

Returns:

Type Description ndarray

A score array aligned with self.item_ids.

docs.title: Install
docs.text:
pip install streamlit-recommenders

Python 3.10 or newer. The install includes what the examples need (scipy for training the baselines, kagglehub for goodbooks). From source, with test tooling:

git clone https://github.com/vaclavstibor/streamlit-recommenders.git
cd streamlit-recommenders
pip install -e ".[dev]"

docs.title: Prepare a dataset
docs.text:
python -m streamlit_recommenders.data.prepare --dataset ml-latest-small

This creates data/ml-latest-small/ with items.csv and interactions.csv. Posters, other datasets, API keys and Windows notes are in Datasets.

docs.title: Your first demo
docs.text:
Save as app.py:

import streamlit_recommenders as sr

items, train, test = sr.load_dataset("data/ml-latest-small")
POPULARITY = train["item_id"].value_counts().index.tolist()

def get_recommendations(user_id, k, session_items=None, **params):
    exclude = set(session_items or [])
    return [item_id for item_id in POPULARITY if item_id not in exclude][:k]

sr.run(get_recommendations=get_recommendations, items=items, interactions=train)

streamlit run app.py

Pick a user in the sidebar (or Try it yourself for an empty profile), click posters to add them to the session, and press Get Recommendations. Replace the function body with your model; the Recommender contract lists the three ways to plug one in.

docs.title: Compare models
docs.text:
Pass a dict of named recommenders. All of them get the same user and session and refresh together. Params can be global or scoped to one model:

sr.run(
    get_recommendations={"Ours": ours, "EASE": ease},
    items=items,
    interactions=train,
    params={
        "num_recs": sr.selectbox("Number of recommendations", [5, 10, 20], index=1),
        "Ours": {"alpha": sr.slider("alpha", 0.0, 1.0, 0.5)},
    },
)

alpha reaches ours.get_recommendations(..., alpha=...) and changes when the slider moves.

Next: the Examples page runs the bundled demos (in-app baselines, exported artifacts, the swipe deck).

docs.title: The session loop
docs.text:
You provide the tables and a recommender. The library keeps the session profile, calls the recommender through a cache, and renders the result. Clicks, likes, dislikes and skips go back into the profile, and the next refresh scores against it.

flowchart LR
  subgraph YOU["you provide"]
    d["items · interactions"]
    f["get_recommendations()"]
  end
  subgraph LIB["the library"]
    s["session profile"]
    c["cache + adapter"]
    lay["layouts: rows · grid · cards"]
  end
  YOU --> LIB --> UI["browser"]
  UI -. "click · like · dislike · skip" .-> s

One refresh: sidebar params and the selected user go to the cached get_recommendations() (through the adapter, which drops arguments the function does not declare); the returned ids are stored per section in session state and rendered. Get Recommendations recomputes every section against the same profile, which is what makes compared models comparable.

docs.title: Module map
docs.text:
flowchart TB
  run["runner.py · sr.run"]
  data["data/ · loaders, prepare (MovieLens, goodbooks, TMDB)"]
  subgraph contract["contract"]
    models["models/ · protocol, adapter"]
    recs["recommenders/ · BaseRecommender, ArtifactRecommender"]
  end
  subgraph runtime["runtime/ (internal)"]
    rt["cache · state · seen · compare · keys"]
  end
  subgraph present["presentation"]
    layouts["layouts/ · rows, grid, cards"]
    widgets["widgets/ · params, profile strips"]
    viz["viz/ · plots, dataset_info"]
    extras["metrics/ · evaluate   content/ · markdown"]
  end
  config["config/ · YAML overrides"] --> run
  data --> run
  run --> contract
  run --> runtime
  run --> present

Training is deliberately outside: the library standardizes how a trained recommender is shown and probed, not how it is trained.

docs.title: Data contract
docs.text: Plain pandas tables, shaped like an offline experiment, so existing data usually fits as is.

docs.title: Tables
docs.text:
Table Required columns Optional columns items item_id title, image_url, description, any metadata interactions / train / test user_id, item_id rating, timestamp users user_id any profile columns

Only items is required. interactions provides user history and the user picker; without it the sidebar picks an item id as context instead. test is for your own evaluation with sr.evaluate. No training happens inside the demo.

dataset = sr.Dataset(items=items, interactions=train, users=users, test=test)
dataset.validate()  # required columns + every referenced id exists

docs.title: Display columns
docs.text:
Column Used for If missing title card hover text, profile strips the item_id image_url poster bundled placeholder image description card hover text the title

Other columns (genres, year, tmdb_id, …) are ignored by the UI and remain available to your body() code.

docs.title: Other column names
docs.text: The defaults are user_id, item_id, rating, timestamp, title, image_url, description. ColumnMap maps other names for validation (sr.Dataset, sr.load_dataset_from_paths), and sr.run(item_columns={"id": ..., "title": ..., "image": ..., "description": ...}) does the same for the cards. The recommender classes and the session logic read user_id/item_id directly, so renaming the DataFrame columns is usually simpler.

docs.title: Prepared folders
docs.text:
items, interactions, test = sr.load_dataset("data/ml-latest-small")

Reads items.csv, then train_interactions.csv if it exists, otherwise interactions.csv, plus an optional test_interactions.csv. Relative poster paths are resolved against the folder. The Datasets guide shows how to create such folders.

docs.title: Feedback & session
docs.text: What happens to a click, Like, Dislike or Skip, and what your model receives because of it.

docs.title: The user profile
docs.text: A model scores against a profile: the selected user's history (their rows in interactions) plus the items liked or clicked in the current session. The Try it yourself user has no history, so its profile is only what you pick.

docs.title: Feedback signals
docs.text:
Action Your model receives BaseRecommender / ArtifactRecommender Click a card / Like the id in session_items (plus a selections entry) adds it to the profile Dislike (cards only) a selections entry with sentiment: "dislike" treats it as seen and passes it to scores(disliked_items=...) Skip (cards only) nothing; the card is filtered out of the deck —

Results refresh on Get Recommendations (rows, grid) or every swipes_per_refresh swipes (cards).

docs.title: How a Dislike changes the ranking
docs.text:
ArtifactRecommender subtracts dislike_weight (default 1.0) times the disliked item's weight row from the scores. For item-item models (ItemKNN, EASE) that pushes down items similar to the rejected one; for sequential CF it pushes down items that usually follow it. With dislike_weight=0 a dislike only hides the item. On ml-latest-small with EASE, after liking Toy Story and A Bug's Life, disliking Toy Story 2 drops The Lion King and Beauty and the Beast from the top 8.

Dislikes do not form a profile on their own: a session with dislikes but no likes still gets the popularity fallback, labeled as such (see below).

To use dislikes in your own model, either declare disliked_items in a BaseRecommender.scores() override, or read selections in a plain function:

def get_recommendations(user_id, k, session_items=None, selections=None, **params):
    disliked = {s["item_id"] for s in selections or [] if s.get("sentiment") == "dislike"}
    ...

Expose the weight as a sidebar control with params={"dislike_weight": sr.slider("Dislike weight", 0.0, 3.0, 1.0)}.

In body() the same state is readable through sr.selected_items(), sr.disliked_items(), sr.displayed_items(label), sr.selections(), sr.current_user() and sr.param_value(name).

docs.title: Seen items
docs.text: By default, items in the user's history or current session (including dislikes) are filtered out. Turn off Hide already-seen items in the sidebar to see the model's raw ranking. The toggle applies to BaseRecommender and ArtifactRecommender; a plain function does its own filtering and receives the flag as hide_seen if it declares it.

docs.title: Nothing is silently attributed to the model
docs.text:
Two situations would otherwise show items the model did not choose. Both are labeled in the UI:

  • Empty session profile. Before the Try it yourself user picks anything, the app shows a sample of popular catalog items, marked as a seed sample. The model is not called until there is something in the profile.
  • Popularity fallback. When an ArtifactRecommender has no signal for the profile (ids outside its catalog, only dislikes, a sequential anchor without transitions), it returns global popularity and the section shows a Popularity fallback warning. ArtifactRecommender.fallback_reason() reports the same thing in code.

docs.title: What is automatic and what you add
docs.text: sr.run always renders the user picker, profile strips, recommendation sections (one per model), sidebar controls from params, and the seen/fallback labels. Everything else is a helper you call inside intro() (above the app) or body() (below it): metric tables, plots, Markdown. The framework never computes metrics or draws charts on its own. Built-in charts are interactive Plotly figures; any other Streamlit element works in body() too.

docs.title: Layouts
docs.text:
Layout Shows rows one horizontally scrolling row of poster cards per model; used for comparison grid n_rows × n_cols posters for browsing one model cards one card at a time with Like / Dislike / Skip, refreshed every swipes_per_refresh swipes

Passing several models (get_recommendations={...}) always uses rows; cards is single-model.

docs.title: Metrics
docs.text:
Hit rate, recall, NDCG, MRR and catalog coverage over held-out interactions:

recs = {"EASE": {user: ease.get_recommendations(user, 10) for user in test.user_id.unique()}}
metrics = sr.evaluate(recs, test_interactions=test, k=10, all_item_ids=items.item_id)
sr.table(metrics)
sr.plot_metric_comparison(metrics)

docs.title: Plots
docs.text:
sr.dataset_info(items, train)  # table sizes; genre, activity and rating distributions
sr.plot_overlap_heatmap(sr.recommendation_overlap_matrix(sr.displayed_items()))  # Jaccard overlap of what is on screen
sr.plot_score_distribution(ease.score_frame(sr.current_user()))  # needs a "score" column

sr.displayed_items() returns exactly the lists on screen, so plots in body() match what the viewer sees.

docs.title: Recommender contract
docs.text:
The boundary between your model and the library is one function:

def get_recommendations(
    user_id: str | int,
    k: int,
    session_items: list[str | int] | None = None,
    selections: list[dict] | None = None,
    **params,
) -> list[str | int]:
    ...

It returns up to k item ids, best first. Ids missing from items are skipped when rendering. params holds the sidebar values (minus the reserved keys).

Optional arguments are passed only if your signature declares them (or takes **params), so a minimal function stays minimal:

Argument Content session_items ids liked or clicked in this session, in order selections per-section {item_id, rank, source} entries; swipe dislikes carry sentiment: "dislike" hide_seen state of the Hide already-seen items toggle

What the model does with them is up to you; Feedback & session describes what the built-in classes do.

docs.title: 1. A plain function
docs.text:
Wrap any scorer, service or API:

def get_recommendations(user_id, k, session_items=None, **params):
    return my_scorer.rank(user_id, session_items=session_items)[:k]

docs.title: 2. Subclass BaseRecommender
docs.text:
Implement scores(), returning one score per entry of self.item_ids. The base class removes seen items and takes the top k:

class MyModel(sr.BaseRecommender):
    def __init__(self, interactions, item_ids):
        self.interactions = interactions  # used to find seen items
        self.item_ids = item_ids

    def scores(self, user_id, session_items=None, disliked_items=None, **params):
        return my_score_vector(user_id, session_items, disliked_items)

disliked_items is optional: declare it to receive the session's swipe dislikes.

docs.title: 3. Load exported weights with ArtifactRecommender
docs.text:
Train elsewhere, export .npz arrays, and the demo only loads them:

models = sr.load_artifacts({"EASE": "artifacts/ease.npz"}, interactions=train)
sr.run(get_recommendations=models, items=items, interactions=train)

The file format is in Training & artifacts.

docs.title: No models in the package
docs.text: The package contains the contract, BaseRecommender and the ArtifactRecommender loader, nothing else. ItemKNN, EASE and Sequential CF are in examples/reference_recommenders.py to copy from. Models trained in RecBole, Cornac, RecPack, LensKit or Elliot connect through the same function instead of becoming dependencies.

docs.title: Reserved params
docs.text:
These params keys configure the app and are not forwarded to the model:

Key Purpose num_recs / k number of recommendations, passed as k layout rows, grid or cards n_cols / n_rows grid size swipes_per_refresh swipes before the cards deck refreshes

docs.title: Training & artifacts
docs.text: The demo does not train models. Train outside, export plain NumPy arrays, and the app only loads them, so no training code or framework ends up in the demo.

docs.title: Export the baselines
docs.text:
python examples/train_baseline_artifacts.py --data data/ml-latest-small

Reads items.csv/interactions.csv (or raw MovieLens movies.csv/ratings.csv), writes train_interactions.csv/test_interactions.csv if they are missing, and saves artifacts/itemknn.npz, artifacts/ease.npz and artifacts/sequential_cf.npz.

docs.title: Artifact format
docs.text:
An artifact stores item-item weights, not user-item scores or embeddings.

Key Shape Meaning model_type (1,) string "itemknn", "ease" or "sequential_cf"; selects the scoring rule item_ids (n_items,) catalog order of the rows and columns below weights (n_items, n_items) float32 cosine similarities, EASE weights, or row-normalized transitions popularity (n_items,) float32 fallback scores when the profile has no signal l2 (EASE only) (1,) float32 regularization, kept for provenance; not read by the loader 
models = sr.load_artifacts({"EASE": "artifacts/ease.npz"}, interactions=train)

How ArtifactRecommender scores:

  • itemknn, ease: a binary vector over history + session items (optionally limited by a history_window param) times weights.
  • sequential_cf: the weights row of the most recent item.
  • Each session dislike subtracts dislike_weight × its weights row.
  • No usable signal: popularity, flagged in the UI and by fallback_reason().

Any model that fits these four arrays can be exported the same way and loaded without code changes.

docs.title: Bring an externally trained model
docs.text:
Models from RecBole, Cornac, RecPack, LensKit, Elliot or a paper repository need no artifact; wrap the trained object in the contract:

class TrainedModelAdapter:
    def __init__(self, model):
        self.model = model

    def get_recommendations(self, user_id, k, session_items=None, **params):
        return self.model.rank(user_id, session_items=session_items)[:k]

sr.run(get_recommendations={"Ours": TrainedModelAdapter(model), "EASE": ease}, items=items, interactions=train)

docs.title: Reference baselines
docs.text:
The same three families as in-app BaseRecommender subclasses, in examples/reference_recommenders.py:

Family Class Reference Item-item CF ItemKNNRecommender Deshpande & Karypis, ACM TOIS 2004 Linear autoencoder EASERecommender Steck, WWW 2019 Sequential CF SequentialCFRecommender first-order item transitions

docs.title: Datasets
docs.text: Every preparation command writes the same layout (items.csv, interactions.csv, raw files) to data/<dataset-name>/ and marks the folder complete in dataset.json, so running it again does nothing unless you pass --force.

docs.title: MovieLens
docs.text:
ml-latest-small, ml-latest, ml-25m and ml-32m, downloaded from GroupLens without an account:

python -m streamlit_recommenders.data.prepare --dataset ml-latest-small

MovieLens has no images. With a free TMDB API key, --with-posters adds posters and plot descriptions (--poster-limit 1000 for a shorter first run):

python -m streamlit_recommenders.data.prepare --dataset ml-latest-small --with-posters

Requests are retried on rate limits and network errors, and items still missing a poster or description are listed in metadata_completeness.csv. Adding --with-posters to an already prepared folder rebuilds it with posters, reusing the downloaded files.

docs.title: goodbooks-10k
docs.text:
Covers are URLs inside the dataset, so there is no enrichment step. The download goes through kagglehub, installed with the library:

python -m streamlit_recommenders.data.prepare --dataset goodbooks
SR_DATA_DIR=data/goodbooks-10k streamlit run examples/compare_models_rows.py

The dataset is public and usually needs no Kaggle login; if yours asks for one, use ~/.kaggle/kaggle.json or KAGGLE_USERNAME/KAGGLE_KEY. You can also put books.csv and ratings.csv into data/goodbooks-10k/ yourself.

docs.title: From Python
docs.text:
sr.prepare_movielens("ml-latest-small", with_posters=True)
sr.prepare_goodbooks()

docs.title: Keys and environment variables
docs.text:
The preparation CLI reads a .env file in the working directory (copy .env.example): TMDB_API_KEY or TMDB_BEARER_TOKEN, and optionally KAGGLE_USERNAME/KAGGLE_KEY. Variables already set in the shell win over .env.

The example apps do not read .env; they take SR_DATA_DIR from the shell and default to data/ml-latest-small:

SR_DATA_DIR=data/goodbooks-10k streamlit run examples/compare_models_rows.py

Windows

VAR=value command is bash syntax. In PowerShell run $env:SR_DATA_DIR="data/goodbooks-10k" first, in cmd set SR_DATA_DIR=data/goodbooks-10k. Downloads verify HTTPS against the system certificate store plus the certifi bundle, so the CERTIFICATE_VERIFY_FAILED error that older releases hit on Windows is fixed without disabling verification.

docs.title: Your own data
docs.text: Write items.csv and interactions.csv following the Data contract into data/<name>/ and set SR_DATA_DIR=data/<name>. Items without images get a placeholder. Keep datasets and posters out of git; commit only the scripts that recreate them.

docs.title: Examples
docs.text:
One runnable example per way of plugging in a model. All of them use the MovieLens sample:

python -m streamlit_recommenders.data.prepare --dataset ml-latest-small
Plug-in form Files When it fits Plain function your app.py (Getting started) you already have something that ranks items BaseRecommender subclass reference_recommenders.py you write the scoring yourself ArtifactRecommender train_baseline_artifacts.py, then compare_models_rows.py, compare_models_grid.py, swipe_deck_cards.py you train elsewhere and only load weights

All examples read the dataset folder from SR_DATA_DIR (default data/ml-latest-small).

docs.title: BaseRecommender: fit in the app
docs.text:
streamlit run examples/reference_recommenders.py

Fits ItemKNN, EASE and Sequential CF at startup and shows them side by side. Each class only implements scores(user_id, session_items, **params); copy one as a starting point.

Memory

In-memory fitting builds dense float64 item × item matrices: about 0.76 GB each for the 9,742 movies of the sample, and EASE holds several while solving. On a machine with a few GB free this can be killed; use the artifact route below instead.

docs.title: ArtifactRecommender: train once, then only load
docs.text:
python examples/train_baseline_artifacts.py --data data/ml-latest-small   # writes artifacts/*.npz
streamlit run examples/compare_models_rows.py    # three models side by side
streamlit run examples/compare_models_grid.py    # one model at a time, chosen in the sidebar
streamlit run examples/swipe_deck_cards.py       # EASE as a swipe deck

No training code runs in these apps; they call sr.load_artifacts({...}, TRAIN) and nothing else model-related. The swipe deck adds a Dislike weight slider: at 0 a dislike only hides the card, higher values push down movies similar to it (see Feedback & session).

docs.title: A model trained somewhere else
docs.text: Models from RecBole, Cornac, LensKit or a paper repository need no artifacts; wrap them in the contract as shown in Training & artifacts.
